title: Imam al-Shafi'i
hook: a descendant of the Prophet's clan, who studied with Malik and the Hanafis

segments.voice: Yesterday, North and West Africa, and your line: hands at the sides. Did you catch yourself about to call something wrong that was only different? Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

A young man arrives in Medina already knowing a book by heart. It's Malik's Muwatta, and the story goes that he memorized it before he ever met its author. He sits in Malik's circle and reads it back to him. Years later the same man is in Iraq, reading the books of al-Shaybani, Abu Hanifa's student, and arguing with the Hanafis face to face. The two great ways of doing law we've spent this week on, Medina's and Kufa's, both pass through one mind. What comes out the other side is a third school, and a new way of asking how law should be found at all. Today: Imam al-Shafi'i.
screen: `THE MUWATTA, BY HEART.` → `MALIK'S CIRCLE, THEN IRAQ.` → `BOTH WAYS THROUGH ONE MIND.`

segments.voice: First, his family. His name is Muhammad ibn Idris, called al-Shafi'i after an ancestor named Shafi'. He was of Quraysh, the Prophet's tribe, from the line of al-Muttalib, a brother of Hashim, who was great-grandfather to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. So his family tree and the Prophet's meet a few generations back. Yet his biographers say he grew up an orphan, poor, in Mecca, with a mother who couldn't afford paper. Next, his teachers. He learned the Qur'an and Arabic in Mecca, then went to Malik in Medina and studied with him. Later, in Iraq, he studied the Hanafi books, and tradition says he learned from al-Shaybani in person. So he had sat with the imam of Medina and read the people of reasoned judgment closely. That's the index line: learned from both. Then what he did with both. He didn't simply blend them. He asked what each was doing and why, and wrote it down as a method. From Malik he kept the hadith at the center. From the Hanafis he kept careful reasoning. He argued with both, and he ended his days in Egypt, where his tomb stands in Cairo. Last, a look back over the week. The Hanafi school's map, with two times for Asr. Abu Hanifa refusing the judge's seat. Malik on foot in Medina, saying I don't know. The Muwatta, the well-trodden path. Medina's living practice. Hands at the sides from Fez to Kano. And now a student who carried both Kufa and Medina, and asked how they fit. The Qur'an gives a short line for students like him: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
screen: `OF QURAYSH, AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.` · `MALIK IN MEDINA, THE HANAFIS IN IRAQ.` · `NOT A BLEND: A METHOD.` · `A WEEK OF TWO SCHOOLS, AND A THIRD.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn from two teachers. Bring to mind two people who taught you the same thing in different ways. Two grandparents who cooked the same dish. Two coaches. A parent who explained and a parent who showed. Hold the first, then the second. What did each get right? Where did they disagree? Now notice what you do today, and see how much of each is in it. If you pray, you can say the line from Surah Ta Ha: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge. If not, simply rest with both faces in mind. The bell holds the time.
Imam al-Shafi'i. A scholar of Quraysh who studied with Malik and with the Hanafis, and founded the Shafi'i school. Today's word.
Your line: learned from both. Today, when two people you respect disagree, ask what each is right about before you pick a side. Day one thousand one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Shafi'i Muslims, across places such as Egypt, East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia, follow the school of Imam al-Shafi'i, who studied with Malik in Medina and with Hanafi scholars in Iraq.

original.note: Arabic: al-Shafi'i, 'the one of Shafi',' named after an ancestor.

Studying with al-Shaybani in person in Iraq: told as 'tradition says'; confirm.
